body_markdown:
Children’s book author


**Julia Donaldson** ’s


*Gruffalo* stories have become a beloved tradition for families in the U.K. and beyond. This week, Spotify’s London headquarters transformed into the Deep Dark Wood as part of the Gruffalo Family Celebration, in honor of Julia’s latest book,


[Gruffalo Granny](https://open.spotify.com/show/4a8ddAXgkbSL3zoIMasFTB) .


The event brought together over 100 guests including families, publishing partners, and more who all had the chance to explore the


*Gruffalo* universe during an afternoon dedicated to the power of children’s stories.


The fun kicked off with a musical moment as Julia performed “


[Funny Face](https://open.spotify.com/track/5gMeiv8dVeF3e4ph7tIg0p?si=ca9cd05738ee4e23) ” and “


[The Squash and the Squeeze](https://open.spotify.com/track/14ZBUUlh1lVbvmWnE4lhWV?si=8c8ca40f13e548f8) ,” accompanied by her son


**Alastair** . Later, she answered questions from some of the curious young audience members, before delighting them with a reading from Gruffalo Granny, and spending time meeting them and signing their books.


Guests also explored the Little Mouse Library and Listening Lounge, cozy spaces where families could discover stories together. At the Gruffalo Cave Craft Area, young guests were encouraged to decorate paper leaves and add them to a story tree. And because food is central to Julia’s books and especially


*Gruffalo Granny* , there were plenty of snacks inspired by the


*Gruffalo* world, too.


NEXT


During the event, we asked Julia about returning to the series after 20 years and the role music has played in her work.


### ***Gruffalo Granny*** **introduces a new generation to one of the U.K.’s most beloved storybook families. What made this the right time to come back to the Deep Dark Wood?**


I think of ideas like little seeds that go in the ground, and you don’t know how long it will take them to germinate. In


*Gruffalo Granny* ’s


case, it just took 25 years.


### **Your stories are often shared out loud: read aloud at bedtime, performed in the classroom, and now as an audiobook. How does the audiobook format change how the story is experienced?**


When Mum, Dad, Grandma, or Grandpa reads a book out loud, they’re often doing the different voices for the characters. You get a similar experience with audiobooks, but instead of the words following the illustrations, kids get to imagine the stories in their heads.


### **Music and performance have always been part of your work. How does rhythm, rhyme, and song help bring a story to life for young audiences?**


I think children who listen to the stories, even very young children, don’t necessarily understand them, but can still enjoy the cadences and the rhythm. In fact, I was recently sent a video of a child who was younger than 2 reciting my book


[Room On The Broom](https://open.spotify.com/show/1Wf3oddIP2TSsT9B5x9jTG) . She didn’t get all the words right, but she got the rhythm and the lyricism of it perfectly.


### **You were a songwriter first before also becoming a children’s storybook author. How do those two worlds overlap for you?**


In some ways, it was easier to make songs because they didn’t have to tell a story. With a song, as long as you have a chorus and you make sure that the last verse is the most punchy, you don’t have to have a whole narrative. But even when I’m writing a story, when it is in rhyme, I want it to be a bit like a song. I don’t want it just to be endless doggerel verse. It has to have some sort of shape, and perhaps a little chorus.


### **So many parents have their own special** ***Gruffalo*** **memories. What does it mean to you to see your characters become part of families’ shared storytelling traditions?**


It’s lovely because I loved reading stories to my own children. It’s nice to feel that I’m contributing to that experience.


*Explore more stories for young readers in our*[Kids & Families audiobook hub](https://open.spotify.com/genre/0JQ5DAqbMKFFp5otF4xkRk) *.*
